Modern.brandNameRationale: Three words. Little names the customer (the baby) and the size of the brand at the same time. & Co. closes it like a small, considered house. The whole name feels modern, warm, and slightly old-fashioned, which is the register parents want for the early years.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern baby brands have moved past the pastel-and-stork aesthetic. Parents want product that looks at home in a modern apartment, doesn't shout at them, and lasts long enough to hand down. The category is asking for design-led brands that respect the parent as a design-literate adult.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Lalo (meetlalo.com) holds the modern baby furniture position. Maisonette (maisonette.com) sits in the design-led marketplace tier. Lovevery (lovevery.com) does the play-and-development middle. Babylist (babylist.com) holds the registry side. We sit closest to Lalo in tone.
Modern.positioningStatement: Baby products designed for parents who don't want their home to look like a nursery.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 42. First-time or second-time parents. Already shop at design-led adult brands. Will pay a premium for baby product that looks like the rest of their house.

dos: Talk to the parent as an adult
Show the product in real homes
Confirm orders in a short, warm note

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. LITTLE & CO. in a tight modern serif, all caps, three words on one line. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the brand's hallmark, used on hangtags, packaging seals, and the social profile.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two names, joined by an ampersand. Avery and Wren both work as first names for any child, suggesting a small heirloom house named for two children who started the catalog. The pair reads as a quiet heritage brand making things to be passed down.
Luxury.story: Avery & Wren began with a single seamstress making clothes for her own children, then for her sister's children, then for friends. The brand has stayed small by intention. Each piece is hand-finished. Some clients are now buying for the second generation.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end children's clothing has been moving toward fashion-forward design and faster collections. There's a parallel market for heirloom-quality pieces in the older tradition. Hand-finished, slowly made, passed down. The customer is paying for the seamstress, the fabric, and the next garment in five years.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Bonpoint (bonpoint.com) holds the institutional Parisian luxury kidswear position. Caramel Baby & Child (caramel-shop.co.uk) sits in the contemporary peer tier. Marlo Kids (marlokids.com) does the design-led artisanal middle. Misha & Puff (mishaandpuff.com) is closest in spirit, with a more design-led brand.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small heritage house making hand-finished clothes for children.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often grandparents buying for grandchildren. Values the quality of the make. Expects the piece to be handed down. Pays in cash and waits months for the order.

dos: Name the fabric and the seamstress
Send a paper letter with each order

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. New is what every baby is. The brand sits on the most universal description of the customer. Plain, honest, and slightly disarming in a category that usually over-decorates.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most baby brands have elaborate names, mascots, and lifestyles. There's an opening for one that strips it all back to the most basic word for the customer.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most baby brands fail this purity test. The closest peer in spirit is some early Japanese baby-clothing brands and the no-name aesthetic of Muji's baby line.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Baby essentials. Plain packaging. Small catalog.

targetAudience.primary: Parents who don't want a brand for their baby. They want a soft cotton onesie, a well-made bib, a swaddle that doesn't fall apart. They want the product and the receipt.

dos: Show the product, the size, the price
Confirm the order in one line

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Stanford sounds like a real surname or place name with quiet institutional weight. Kids Group names the holding-company category. The whole name reads like a real, established children's-products distributor already on the procurement panel at every major children's retailer.
Corporate.industrySummary: Children's products distribution and licensing is a serious B2B category. Major retailers, specialty children's chains, and brand licensors need wholesale partners who can deliver across toys, apparel, gear, and accessories. The category is mostly served by huge giants and a few specialist firms.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Mattel (mattel.com) holds the institutional toy peer. Hasbro (hasbro.com) sits in the same tier. Spin Master (spinmaster.com) is the modern challenger. We sit smaller, focused on the contemporary children's-brand operator side.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Wholesale distribution and brand licensing for the contemporary children's category.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Retailers and brand licensees want partners who can deliver children's product with operational discipline and design-led category development. We sit between the giants (slow, brand-heavy) and the boutique brands (lacking scale).

targetAudience.primary: Category buyers, VPs of Merchandising, and licensing directors at children's retail chains, specialty toy stores, and direct-to-consumer kids brands. They sign multi-season contracts.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Tiny Gang names the customer and the brand at the same time. The phrase belongs to how parents actually talk about their kids: gang, crew, posse. Loud, warm, playful, and slightly mischievous.
Creative.manifesto: Most baby brands sell a calm, soft, beige version of parenting. We made Tiny Gang for the parents who have a different version. The one where the kid is loud, opinionated, mostly sticky, and the parent is exhausted, smitten, and still funny. The brand is for the actual experience of having small children.
Creative.industrySummary: Children's branding has been calm, beige, and Instagram-ready. There's room for a brand that's loud, warm, sticker-friendly, and serious about making products that work for kids who are also loud.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Hunter Bell (hunterbell.com), if it operated in baby, would be the closest. Goldfish Kiss (goldfishkiss.com) does playful well. Magnetic Me (magneticme.com) holds the functional middle. We sit louder than all of them, with a clearer point of view.
Creative.positioningStatement: A children's brand for loud kids and tired parents.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 45. Parents of toddlers and small children. Tired. Funny. Already have one kid in stickers. Buy the brand because the marketing made them laugh.

dos: Quote real customer complaints (with permission and humor)
Talk to the parent who hasn't slept
donts: Photograph children sleeping peacefully on white sheets
